Today at Connect, we announced Ray-Ban Meta Audio, our first-ever audio glasses, and our biggest expansion of AI glasses yet through our partnership with EssilorLuxottica.
We’re building AI glasses for everyone. By the end of the year, we’ll offer more than 100 different glasses options across Ray-Ban, Oakley, and Meta Glasses, including lightweight frames made for all-day wear and new styles with slimmer designs and longer battery life. And with regular software updates, new AI features, and our growing ecosystem of apps and experiences, these glasses will only keep getting better.
AI glasses help you on the go, from giving you sports scores and local restaurant picks to translating live conversations. With a connection to your personal AI agent from Muse , they’ll offer more ways than ever to help you manage your daily life — whether you’re building healthy habits or navigating a busy calendar — all without reaching for your phone.
Audio has been our most popular feature since day one because our glasses give you high-quality sound without closing you off from the world around you. Our new Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses pack the power of earbuds and AI into our lightest and slimmest AI glasses yet, in iconic Ray-Ban style.
At just 43 grams, Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses are light enough to wear all day, and offer maximum comfort with professional-adjustable temple tips, adjustable or swappable nose pads, and overextension hinges. You can listen to music and podcasts, take calls that capture your voice more clearly than earbuds, and talk with your AI assistant hands-free for up to 12 hours on a single charge, with up to an additional 48 hours from the included charging case.
They come in 23 color and lens combinations across two new styles: Clubmaster, an iconic Ray-Ban style with a retro-inspired silhouette, and Burbank, a classic, timeless rectangle style. Both are compatible with a wide range of optical prescriptions.
You can pre-order a pair today starting at $349 USD and they ship October 13.
Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) is the next generation of the world’s best-selling AI glasses. In support of our vision to make great-looking glasses first, we’ve packed the tech Ray-Ban Meta wearers love into a slimmer, more comfortable design, with longer battery life and a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI.
With Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3), we’re giving people more choice than ever. They come in 27 color and lens combinations across 3 styles: Aviator, Zena (a bold new cat-eye frame), and Wayfarer. And to mark the 90th anniversary of the Ray-Ban Aviator, we’re releasing a limited-edition Aviator in a vintage-inspired colorway.
Gen 3 gets up to nine hours of battery life (an hour more than Gen 2) plus professional-adjustable temple tips for a better fit. A new 6-mic array cuts more than 90% of background noise, so calls and voice commands are crisp and clear, even on windy or crowded streets.
With a 12 MP camera and 3K Ultra HD video recording, you can capture photos and videos hands-free to save and share with others, and with new dynamic photos, you get to choose the best frame, so you get a standout picture every time. As with every generation of the glasses, these feature a built-in LED light that helps make people around you aware if you’re taking photos or video.
Later this year, Meta AI glasses will be the first consumer devices that enable users to capture and experience videos in Dolby Atmos with 360-degree spatial sound. Just record and your glasses handle everything, so playback feels as immersive as being there.
Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) is available today, with prices starting at $449 USD.
Earlier this year, we launched Meta Glasses in partnership with EssilorLuxottica. We’re now expanding the collection with two new styles, Capri and Nova; giving you more ways to personalize; and bringing them to new markets around the world.
Building on the success of Meta Glasses by Kylie Jenner , we’re releasing a new colorway, Ivory, that’s a fresh take on her signature Starfire style. Starting at $399 USD.

articles.title_zh: MGM Resorts shares sink 11% after Barry Diller's People Inc. rescinds takeover offer
articles.content_orig:
Barry Diller's People Inc. has rescinded its proposal to buy MGM Resorts International , sending shares of the casino giant down roughly 11% on Thursday.
The update comes nearly four months after Diller's company offered to purchase MGM Resorts for $48.30 per share. People Inc. already owns a roughly 26.1% stake in MGM.
Diller, chairman of People Inc. — formerly known as IAC — attributed the decision to the complicated nature of the deal.
"There are lots of ingredients that go into a proposal of this kind on its way to completion," Diller said in the press release. "We didn't feel the mix was coming together in the way we had hoped and have decided not to pursue taking the company private at this time."
CNBC's David Faber reported Thursday that Diller backed off the deal in part because of the significant debt load it would have created for the company.
Still, Diller said he is willing to consider a future deal.
"We at People Incorporated remain open to and interested in the possibility of a strategic transaction with MGM Resorts and look forward to considering a range of alternatives," he said in the release.
Earlier this week, shareholders of Caesars Entertainment approved an offer from billionaire Tilman Fertitta to acquire the casino company for $17.6 billion. Caesars shareholders will receive $31 per share in cash.
— CNBC's Contessa Brewer contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
Week 4 is the biggest weekend of the 2026 college football season.
Saturday features six matchups between teams ranked in the AP Top 25. Four of those come in the SEC and the other two are in the Big Ten. We won't filibuster any longer. Here are the games to watch this weekend.
The winner gets to be called UT for the rest of the year. The loser has to find another acronym.
It's the biggest game of young Tennessee QB Faizon Brandon's career and he's shown why he won the starting QB job as a true freshman through the first three games. Brandon has yet to throw an interception and has nine total touchdowns; he's thrown for six and rushed for three.
Two of those games have come against Furman and Kennesaw State , so it's hard to judge just how good the Volunteers offense actually is this season. But it's a promising sign that Tennessee has been able to dominate its opponents on the ground no matter who it has played. In a 45-24 win over Georgia Tech , the Vols rushed 45 times for 299 yards.
That takes pressure off Brandon; he was 10-of-21 passing for 148 yards and two scores against the Yellow Jackets. Is that run game sustainable against the Longhorns? Teams are averaging just 3.4 yards a carry against Texas this season and Ohio State had 94 yards on 31 carries.
Auburn transfer Cam Coleman hasn't caught more than four passes in a game so far the season for Texas, but he's scored twice against both Texas State and UTSA. Arch Manning is averaging under seven yards an attempt through the first three games of the season and Tennessee's opponents have thrown for just 453 yards all season.
The Rebels' status as an underdog isn't a sign of disrespect to a top-five team. Rather, it's more about how good Florida has looked through the first three weeks of Jon Sumrall's tenure.
The Gators were the clear better team in their win over Auburn as Jadan Baugh has established himself as one of the best running backs in the country. Baugh has 458 yards and eight touchdowns already this season and is averaging 8.5 yards every time he carries the ball. Teams haven't been afraid to run the ball against Ole Miss so far this season, either. Charlotte's 33 attempts are the fewest of any Ole Miss opponent and LSU rushed for 172 yards and two scores in the Rebels' 32-24 win in Week 3.
It's also a potential letdown spot for Ole Miss. The game against LSU was such a focal point since the schedule was released that it's only natural to think the Rebels won't be as up for this game. Will that be rooted in any basis in reality? We'll know on Saturday.
We may also need to wait until Saturday to know about Ole Miss RB Kewan Lacy 's status. He re-injured his surgically repaired left shoulder in the win over LSU and missed the end of the game. JT Lindsey was effective in Lacy's absence, but Ole Miss is a much better football team with its star on the field. Having Lacy out there and effective helps Trinidad Chambliss share the playmaking burden.
This game has all the potential in the world to satiate your desires for old-school football. The over/under of 38.5 is the lowest of any game offered at BetMGM in Week 4.
No one is giving up fewer points per game than Iowa through three weeks. The Hawkeyes have shut out Northern Illinois and Northern Iowa — at least Michigan doesn't have "north" in its name — and allowed 13 points to Iowa State in Week 2. Those three teams have put up just 177 yards per game.
Hank Brown has taken over as Iowa's starting quarterback after a competition with Jeremy Hecklinski that went all the way to Week 1. The former Auburn QB is 45-of-62 passing for 473 yards and three touchdowns. Those are explosive numbers compared to the passing offense that Iowa has had in recent seasons.
The biggest question may actually come at running back, where both Kamari Moulton and L.J. Phillips missed the Week 3 win. Moulton and Phillips are the Hawkeyes' top running backs. Iowa didn't need them against its FCS foe, but will need at least one available on Saturday.
Michigan's offense finally broke free in the second half of a 52-17 win over UTEP in Week 3. After scoring 30 points over the first two weeks of the season, the Wolverines nearly matched that number with four touchdowns in the third quarter alone.
Will that game be a turning point for an offense that had looked stuck for the better part of 10 quarters? There are few questions about the Michigan defense. The ceiling for the Wolverines will be entirely determined by just how good the offense can be.
Some of the luster disappeared from this game as both teams lost in Week 3. Texas A&M's home loss to Kentucky was entirely unexpected. And it wasn't a fluke, either. The Wildcats bossed the Aggies .
Texas A&M lost receiver Terry Bussey for the season with a right leg injury on the opening kickoff. That puts more pressure on Mario Craver and Isaiah Horton to be the primary playmakers for an Aggies passing game that looks to need a robust support system around quarterback Marcel Reed . Craver and Horton have combined to catch 31 of the 62 completions Reed has thrown this season and all but one of his touchdown passes.
Reed emerged as Texas A&M's quarterback in this game two seasons ago as he came off the bench to rush for three scores in a 38-23 win. This season, he's completing less than 60% of his passes.
Sam Leavitt is still looking for his first great game as LSU's starting quarterback. Leavitt has thrown at least one interception in each of the Tigers' first three games and has five interceptions to just three touchdown passes. He's supplemented that total with six rushing touchdowns, but Leavitt needs to be a better passer for the Tigers' playoff hopes to become reality.
And the playoff is going to be a central theme of this game. The loser will drop to 2-2 and likely have no path to the postseason with another loss.
This is another game with some serious playoff implications, especially for an Oregon team that already has a loss thanks to that Week 2 defeat at Oklahoma State.
Even if it'd be a victory over a .500 Oregon team, a win would be a defining one for this Big Ten version of USC. The Trojans haven't threatened to be in the top tier of the conference since making the move from the Pac-12. Yes, there was a home win over Michigan in 2025, but that Wolverines team finished with five losses.
As always, there are still questions about the USC defense. The Trojans shut out Fresno State in a dominant Week 1 performance. But they've otherwise allowed 26 points in each of the other three games and 75 points combined over the past two weeks. The 35 points Rutgers scored in Week 3 was just seven fewer than the Scarlet Knights ' combined total over the first two weeks of the season.
If Oregon's offense has the same tells that it allegedly did against Oklahoma State, former TCU coach Gary Patterson's unit can tee off. But if the Portland State game was some much-needed corrective action, the Ducks could easily be the third straight team to drop 30 or more against the Trojans. If that happens and USC still wins, QB Jayden Maiava is going to get a lot of Heisman love. Through four games, Maiava is completing 76% of his passes for 1,173 yards and 12 TDs to just one interception.
Clemson (1-) at Cal (10:30 p.m. ET Friday, ESPN): We've got some serious ACC-after-dark potential with this one. Cal CB Kingston Lopa added a fifth interception against Wagner in Week 3 and will be licking his chops at the prospect of facing freshman Tait Reynolds in his first road start. Reynolds was much better after Clemson's win over North Carolina resumed following a lengthy weather delay.
Oklahoma at No. 2 Georgia (-14) (3:30 p.m. ET, ESPN): The Sooners are big underdogs as their offense has struggled so far this season. Tackle Michael Fasusi is unlikely to play along with star defensive lineman David Stone . That could be a recipe for disaster against a Georgia team that has dominated everyone it has played so far this season. Will Gunner Stockton

Xi Jinping says China and US must ensure AI ‘is always under human control’ and backs US-Iran deal to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz
At Trump meeting, Xi lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
Here is brief recap of the remarks made by Donald Trump and Xi Jinping just now on the Chinese president’s landmark state visit to Washington.
Trump touted their “truly great friendship” and that they had made “tremendous strides on the issues facing our countries” as he welcomed Xi to the White House. He kept his remarks vague and focused on their personal relationship, of which he said he is “very proud”. Trump said the two leaders would focus on security, technology and artificial intelligence at their summit today, and are working towards “a more balanced trade relationship”.
Xi, meanwhile, struck a very different tone, acknowledging that he and Trump have built a “personal rapport” but concentrating his remarks on geopolitical concerns. Xi called for continued dialogue and the building of mutual trust, understanding and peaceful coexistence between the two countries and to avoid conflict. He stressed that Chinese and US interests are “deeply intertwined” and that they “stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in conflict”. He also stated clearly his hope that Chinese companies would be “treated fairly” in the United States.
The Chinese leader also emphasised their joint, historic responsibility as leading nations in artificial intelligence. Both the US and China have the capability and responsibility to manage AI for good, he stressed, and must “ensure the development of AI is always under human control and serve the wellbeing of the people”.
The two men are meeting now in the Oval Office, where they will discuss the fragile trade-war truce, Taiwan , AI and China’s support for Iran and for Russia’s war in Ukraine. A breakthrough is unlikely today for the world’s two most powerful nations, but stick with us as we bring you all the latest out of the meeting.
The head of ⁠the Airlines for America industry group has said US carriers oppose adding more direct flights from China to America , even as Xi Jinping raised ⁠the idea.
Chris Sununu , ​who heads the group representing American Airlines, United Airlines, Delta Air Lines and others, said US carriers continue to be hampered by the fact that ⁠Chinese counterparts are allowed to overfly Russia on eight flights. He had been advocating to Trump administration officials not to give in, he said on Thursday.
double quotation mark It’s not just a minor ⁠thing. It’s a huge cost to the airlines to have to go around Russia.
At an event in Washington on ‌Thursday, Xi raised the idea ‌of increasing flights, Reuters reports. The US and China currently can each operate about 50 round-trip flights a week.
double quotation mark Our ‌two sides may also increase direct flights to facilitate two-way travel and trade.
The White House did not immediately comment.
Donald Trump has two hours to kill until he hosts a state dinner in honor of China’s president, Xi Jinping , so naturally he used the break to renew his hostilities with two US news outlets he attempted to punish for reporting unflattering details about his presidency.
Writing on his social media platform, Trump complained that two of the three outlets he banned from the White House, CNN and MS Now, “refused to cover” his elaborate welcome of Xi to the White House on Thursday.
“The event was magnificent – Actually made for Television but, because they’re Fake News, and because they knew how good it would be, they didn’t want credit to be given to ‘TRUMP,’ they refused to be there,” the president claimed.
What Trump failed to report to his followers on Truth Social was that the two broadcasters were not in position to cover the event live because his own actions and those of his aides.
Trump’s aides initially failed to give journalists from those news organizations access to the White House on Thursday morning, despite a court order issued before dawn that their passes be restored. Their passes were taken away last week following Trump’s decision to ban them, along with Politico.
Since CNN is also one of the five networks that provide pool video coverage of White House events to other broadcasters, in a rotation determined by the White House press office. The other networks refused to resume normal coverage until they were assured that the White House would restore CNN crews to the broadcast pool. The other networks – ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News – had refused to provide pool video of White House events in solidarity with CNN since Trump attempted to ban the cable news outlet from covering him in person last week.
“At the moment, the pool doesn’t have that assurance, so it has not filmed any of Trump and Xi’s events so far today,” CNN’s chief media analyst, Brian Stelter, reported before Trump, a former reality television star, posted his complaint.
According to China’s Xinhua state news agency, Xi Jinping has said that the Chinese and US economic and trade teams have reached a new joint agreement, which he called “good news for the global economy”.
Xi and Trump also ​exchanged views on the Middle East, Ukraine and ⁠the Korean ​Peninsula during ​the meeting, ​Xinhua reported.
We’ll bring you more on this as we get it.
One is an authoritarian who represses the media with a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party.
Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, Xi Jinping , to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries.
And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico . Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat, described the vivid contrast as “wrong and embarrassing” .
That was hard to deny, given that China ranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index , ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China.
The deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate.
Chuck Schumer , the Democratic minority leader, observed on X : “ If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you… ”
Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet?
Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan.
Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed , of course – before the two delegations, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter.
But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”.
Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower .
But with more flattery, he added:
double quotation mark Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great

articles.content_orig:
Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
Trump-Xi summit – latest updates
Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.
At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain.
Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.
“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.
“We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”
With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.
Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.
His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.
Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president.
“President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said.
Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”
He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.
Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”
Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.”
The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.
Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on.
Trump and Xi were scheduled to hold bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.
Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.
In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.
A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said.
Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.
Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continue to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running.

articles.title_orig: ‘Hostile, but hooked’: What’s behind the US-China trade truce extension?
articles.title_zh: ‘Hostile, but hooked’: What’s behind the US-China trade truce extension?
articles.content_orig:
The red carpet was rolled out, and a trade truce was extended. Yet, beneath the pomp and pageantry of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit with US leader Donald Trump on Thursday, Washington and Beijing remain locked in a much deeper strategic rivalry.
Xi arrived in Washington, DC on Wednesday evening for talks on Thursday, and Trump was there to meet him personally on the tarmac.
The meeting was the first state visit by a Chinese leader to the US in 11 years. But it is also the third time in less than a year that the two men have met face to face, as the two powers remain uneasily gridlocked in competition over AI , rare-earth metals, the question of Taiwan, and the Iran war.
Overhanging it all is the paused, but simmering, trade war between their two nations.
Almost as soon as Trump began his second term in the White House in January 2025, up went tariffs on Chinese goods as he accused China of facilitating the flow of fentanyl, a deadly drug, to the US. Beijing responded with its own levies, then restricted exports of valuable rare-earth metals which are crucial for the development and manufacture of everything high-tech, from smartphones to fighter jets. At one point, tariffs were heading towards 150 percent before being paused to allow time for talks.
Finally, the two leaders called a truce on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in South Korea on October 30, and they met once more, in May, when Trump travelled to Beijing.
As Xi landed in Washington on Wednesday this week, the Trump administration announced that the two countries had agreed to extend an October 2025 truce which had offered some respite from the punishing tariffs, produced an agreement from China to buy more soyabeans from the US and delayed the ban on rare-earth exports from China until January 10. The prospect of a much-longed-for trade deal appeared to be in the air when US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News he had met Chinese ‌Vice Premier He Lifeng before Xi’s visit to “see if we could ⁠do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series ⁠of smaller things”.
But analysts have, for the most part, shot down such hopes. Beyond tariffs, they say, the simmering conflict between the two powers now encompasses new US sanctions on buyers of Russian oil – namely China – and sweeping investment and research restrictions, never mind the intensifying race for dominance in artificial intelligence .
“The two-month extension isn’t a bridge to a grand bargain – it’s a temporary sandbag holding back a structural flood,” Beijing-based Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Center for International Governance Innovation, told Al Jazeera.
In fact, the truce is little more than “transactional theatre” – an attempt at good optics before the upcoming US midterm elections – Tangen said.
Trump’s deeply unpopular war on Iran has already inflicted severe damage to his chances in that vote. Democrats are leading in the polls amid concerns about the rising cost of energy, triggered by the war which the US started. Trump ultimately needs wins on other issues.
The current truce with China serves a purpose, therefore, but is fragile enough to be undone the moment political utility shifts for Trump, Tangen said.
“Success in January won’t be measured by what is solved, but by whether the knot is left tight enough to hold, but not kill,” said Tangen.
Phillippe Le Corre, professor of international relations and Asian studies at France’s ESSEC Business School, said the length of the truce extension indicates clearly that a more permanent deal remains out of grasp.
“The extensions are getting shorter and shorter, which means they haven’t found a common ground on many issues,” Le Corre told Al Jazeera.
“The two-month extension is a terrible outcome for the US. Nothing is resolved, and many Damocles’ swords are still hanging over Washington’s head,” he added.
Trump’s entire China policy, Le Corre argued, is in fact short-sighted. “That is bringing the world a lot of uncertainty,” he said.
Some analysts are more hopeful, but not much. Sun Chenghao, a fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, described the extension of the trade truce as a “useful interim step”. It shows that both sides want to preserve the recent easing of tensions, which is meaningful progress, he said.
“From China’s perspective, a sustainable agreement needs reciprocal benefits and greater policy predictability,” Sun told Al Jazeera. “Additional purchases cannot indefinitely compensate for uncertainty over tariffs, technology restrictions and market access.”
The extension’s value, however, will depend on whether it produces “concrete commitments” from Beijing and Washington, Sun added.
There is motivation to get a deal done, analysts say. Any escalation in the US-China trade war will be costly for both sides.
But there is some way to go. A Congressional Research Service report in July 2026 noted that Chinese goods exported to the US still face tariffs of 36.5 percent, while US goods entering China are taxed at 31 percent.
Any higher, and they will raise import and manufacturing costs in the US, squeeze margins and increase pressure on consumer prices, said Sun. They would also hurt US farmers and industrial exporters, he added, just as the US faces pressure from the rising costs of its war on Iran, which have pushed it into a record national debt of $40 trillion two years earlier than expected.
“Washington is playing a high-stakes game of economic chicken with a $40 trillion debt load, an inflationary sword of Damocles, zero fiscal cushion to absorb a truce collapse and a dependence [on] Chinese industrial and manufacturing inputs,” Tangen said.
US consumers and the economy in general will find it tough to survive yet another inflationary shock from renewed tariffs “at a time when the federal budget already operates like a high-wire Ponzi scheme”.
Then there is the AI race, which no one can afford to lose. According to Jon Bateman, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, a partial “decoupling” of US and Chinese technology ecosystems is under way. US policymakers have pushed to become less dependent on Chinese tech and “to secure America’s technological future in the context of a rising China”, Bateman writes.
But that will not help if there is a collapse in valuations of companies in the AI sector, which currently drive global stock markets. An AI valuation collapse, Tangen warned, “could trigger a financial tsunami that makes 2008 look tame – making technological decoupling meaningless as the world is plunged into a depression”.
Despite the trade war and Trump’s tariffs, China’s trade with other countries has risen sharply, with the country registering a $1.2 trillion global trade surplus last year. But an escalation of the trade war with the US would nevertheless spell increased pressure on export orders, employment in exposed industries and business confidence, said Sun.
Beijing does hold one crucial ace card – it is sitting on 60 percent of the world’s known deposits of rare-earth minerals, said Le Corre. It processes 90 percent of them, too. These are the metals that all countries need supplies of for semiconductors, technological components and the manufacture of weapons, to name but a few. Last year, China began to make use of that leverage by restricting exports of five of the 12 rare-earth metals it mines in April. Then, in October, it prepared to restrict seven more – until the trade truce happened. Plans for the export restrictions are not shelved, however, merely on hold.
“[China] understood this over the past year and they are certainly not going to give up on this,” said Le Corre.
“Washington is hostile, but it is hooked,” Tangen said. “You cannot threaten China with secondary sanctions on energy while desperately needing its rare-earths to fuel your military-industrial base.”

articles.content_orig:
Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
Trump-Xi summit – latest updates
Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.
At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain.
Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.
“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.
“We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”
With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.
Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.
His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.
Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president.
“President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said.
Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”
He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.
Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”
Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.”
The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.
Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on.
Trump and Xi were scheduled to hold bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.
Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.
In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.
A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said.
Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.
Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continue to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running.

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

articles.title_orig: US-China Summit begins with signs that the trade truce will stay in place — for now
articles.title_zh: US-China Summit begins with signs that the trade truce will stay in place — for now
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The US-China summit got underway in earnest on Thursday with signals from both sides that importers may be able to count on some stability in the trading relationship between the two nations for the coming few months.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Wednesday that the US and China would extend their current trade truce — set to expire in November — by two months as he set up a new early 2027 deadline for continuing trade talks.
The Chinese didn't immediately confirm that extension, but Chinese President Xi Jinping opened the summit with notably conciliatory remarks on trade. He offered his support, according to a translation, for "a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability" as well as increased flights "to facilitate two-way travel and trade."
A two-month extension could be a letdown for some importers who had been hoping for a one-year extension of the trade pact announced last year in South Korea, but the continuation of current tariff rates and rules for the remainder of 2026 could add a measure of stability.
The extension of the truce will last, Bessent said on Fox News , until Jan. 10, 2027, in order to "to give us more time to see what we can do on the economic front." He has also suggested that a bigger deal with China could be hammered out in the months ahead.
He told reporters in Washington on Wednesday, after a meeting with Vice Premier He Lifeng, that the Chinese "came up with the idea of a bigger deal" and suggested that the US is open to it.
Meanwhile, long-term certainty is more elusive, with both sides keeping options for further provocations on the table.
Trump's team is considering new 7.5% tariffs on China around the issue of overcapacity, but has delayed moving forward until after this week's meeting — and perhaps until after the midterm elections amid withering US public opinion of tariffs.
The current US tariffs on China, according to the Yale Budget Lab , net out to a 26.54% effective statutory tariff rate.
Bessent and Trump have repeatedly stressed that the US is ambivalent and would be happy with either an extension of current trade agreements or new talks.
President Trump said during an opening ceremony on Thursday at the White House that "our teams have been working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship."
At issue is a one-year truce announced in South Korea last October that included provisions suspending some tariffs and promises from the Chinese government on rare earth exports.
The US halved some tariffs on Chinese goods as part of a reset in relations, while China stepped back from its promise to restrict rare earth mineral exports for a year. The deal also included the suspension of some shipping fees , an easing of the US export control rules, and increased Chinese purchases of US soybeans.
Both Bessent and Trump have underlined that soybeans and larger agriculture issues remain priorities for them.
Bessent told Fox that China has been holding up its soybean commitments, but "we think they're a little behind schedule" on other agricultural purchase commitments.
Trump also said a priority during this week's summit is "new market access for American farmers and ranchers."

Our second NFL week of the year is in the books, but unfortunately, it yielded multiple significant injuries, especially at the all-important quarterback position.
After a hot start to the year, New York Giants QB Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury against the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night, for which he will undergo season-ending knee surgery . Jameis Winston is set to start for the Giants for now, though head coach John Harbaugh did not rule out the potential for the team to trade for a veteran .
The Chicago Bears are also expected to be without their starting quarterback for now after Caleb Williams suffered a hamstring injury in Week 2. Head coach Ben Johnson dubbed him "week-to-week" on Monday , though the team did not yet officially rule him out for Week 3. That isn't the end of their quarterback woes, however, as backup Tyson Bagent was placed in the concussion protocol earlier this week, which could force the Bears to start QB3 Case Keenum against the Philadelphia Eagles this week.
Washington Commanders star Jayden Daniels also suffered a significant injury this week after dislocating his elbow for the second time since last season. He's already been ruled out for Week 3 and is expected to miss additional time, though it's unclear how much, as Daniels continues to gather opinions from specialists . Marcus Mariota will get the start in his absence.
One team that is getting past a bad injury is the Falcons. After two weeks of disappointing outings from Cooper Rush , Atlanta announced on Monday that Michael Penix Jr. will start for the Falcons on Thursday against the Packers . A healthy Tua Tagovailoa is reportedly set to back him up.
Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more ahead of Week 3.
Starting Panthers receiver Jalen Coker might be trending the wrong way after suffering an ankle injury. Coker, who was limited in practice on Wednesday, did not practice with Carolina on Thursday.
During the media portion of Thursday's practice, WCNC's Nick Carboni captured Coker walking gingerly off the field.
The Panthers play the Browns on Sunday; at this rate, it seems less likely that Coker will be able to play.
Nick Chubb started his career as a Cleveland Brown, and he'll be ending it that way.
In an interview on ESPN Cleveland's Browns Daily, Haslam Sports Group managing partner JW Johnson announced the Chubb would be joining the team on Friday to officially retire as a Brown. Chubb will participate in a press conference, and will be present on Sunday as Cleveland hosts the Carolina Panthers.
"I'm just thrilled for Nick and proud of him and happy to call him a friend," Johnson said.
Chubb announced his retirement from the NFL in August, bringing his pro career to a somewhat early end. The running back played seven of his eight NFL seasons in Cleveland, spending last season with the Houston Texans.
Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs remains on the NFL's commissioner exempt list . And in the lead-up to his team's Week 3 "Thursday Night Football" clash with the Atlanta Falcons , ESPN's Rob Demovsky reported the latest update involving the case that has sidelined Jacobs indefinitely.
In Wisconsin on Thursday, Brown County District Court Judge Marc A. Hammer denied the victim's request to permanently seal evidence, including the surveillance video the criminal complaint said captured a portion of the May 23 incident at Jacobs' home in Green Bay , as reported by ESPN .
Had the evidence been permanently sealed, the NFL might not have been able to review that video, which could affect the severity of punishment the league hands the three-time Pro Bowler.
The NFL's investigation into the matter is ongoing, and it could result in a suspension for Jacobs, although it's important to note that time served on the commissioner exempt list — which prevents a player from practicing with a team or playing in its games — would count toward a suspension. Jacobs has been on that list since Aug. 30 and, consequently, has missed the Packers' first two games of the 2026 campaign.
On Sept. 10, Jacobs pleaded no contest to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property . He was reportedly convicted of battery and fined $1,000. Additionally, per ESPN , the 28-year-old Jacobs accepted a deferred judgment agreement on the criminal damage to property charge.
Collins missed Week 2 with a hamstring injury and was not spotted as the Texans began practice on Thursday. He also sat out Wednesday and his status for Houston's Week 3 matchup against the Colts does not look promising.
The Ravens look like they will be without wide receiver Zay Flowers for a second straight week as they face the Cowboys in Rio de Janeiro.
Flowers will not practice on Thursday as he deals with a hamstring injury. He was a limited participant in practice last week before being ruled out for Week 2.
There are 220 players with two or more catches this season. Among them: Nate Adkins, Jared Wayne, LaJohntay Wester, Brady Russell, Brevyn Spann-Ford and Lan Larison.
One notable player not on that list of 220: Marvin Harrison Jr.
It's early in the season but there is already a lot of worry about Harrison. It's not just two games. It's 31 largely underwhelming games into his career for the Arizona Cardinals receiver. He has just two 100-yard games. He has one game with more than six catches. And two games into this season he has one catch for 33 yards. The Cardinals threw it 28 times in Week 2 against the Seahawks and Harrison was targeted only once.
Harrison was one of the most exciting receiver prospects ever. He was the fourth overall pick of the 2024 NFL Draft, after three really good quarterbacks (Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, Drake Maye) were picked. Nobody is excited anymore.
San Francisco 49ers receiver Mike Evans did not practice Wednesday due to a hip injury, but it sounds like he'll be OK to play in Week 3, per NFL Network.
Evans' injury is said to be minor and he's expected to return to practice ahead of Week 3.
Evans proved he still had something left in the tank in Week 1, hauling in six catches and scoring a touchdown. He had more receiving yards in Week 2, but left the game early due to his injury. The 49ers were blowing out the Miami Dolphins at the time of the injury, however, so it's possible Evans could have kept playing in a more competitive game.
The Los Angeles Rams may not have Puka Nacua in Week 3. Head coach Sean McVay gave a pessimistic outlook on Nacua's recovery Thursday, saying the wideout is "not making great progress."
McVay made those comments during a radio appearance.
McVay added he has "a ton of confidence" in the remaining receivers if Nacua can't go.
The wideout is battling hip and groin issues and missed Week 2 due to those injuries. When healthy, Nacua is among the best receivers in the game.
A Tuesday MRI proved more daunting, the specter of season-ending surgery suddenly looming over the Giants and their quarterback. By Wednesday, head coach John Harbaugh confirmed multiple reports that the decision was made: Jaxson Dart will undergo surgery to repair damage to his meniscus, MCL and PCL. His ACL is intact.
Harbaugh, whose appreciation for Dart strongly swayed his decision to join the Giants in January, is left to pick up the pieces of an offense now in the hands of Jameis Winston for the rest of the regular season (Harbaugh left open a potential postseason return for Dart).
How much does a head coach's job change when his starting quarterback goes down?

Stroud missed three games last season, Texans backup Davis Mills went 3-0 in his place, keeping them in the playoff race. Two giant pandas from China will arrive at Zoo Atlanta in the coming days, renewing a loan initiative that had lapsed amid diplomatic friction between Beijing and Washington.
Chinese President Xi Jinping confirmed the timeline Thursday after China and the facility said in April that Ping Ping, a male, and Fu Shuang, a female, would travel to the United States.
Xi’s White House statement before talks with President Donald Trump offered the first public confirmation of the schedule. Beijing had recalled four pandas from Atlanta in 2024, ending the last active U.S. panda loans at the time.
Xi said Ping Ping and Fu Shuang "will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people" in "a few days." He described the update as "a piece of good news" and celebrated the program as showing "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."
The animals arrive under a conservation agreement between the zoo and the China Wildlife Conservation Association. Both pandas were born at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding in China.
In 2024, Lun Lun, Yang Yang, Ya Lun, and Xi Lun returned from Zoo Atlanta to China, concluding a 25-year arrangement and leaving the U.S. without any pandas for several months. The National Zoo in Washington sent back three pandas in 2023, receiving Bao Li and Qing Bao in October 2024. Other U.S. facilities previously returned pandas as agreements lapsed.
When Atlanta's pandas were officially promised in the spring, Zoo Atlanta CEO Raymond B. King welcomed "the wonder and joy of giant pandas" and said the zoo was "delighted and honored to yet again be trusted as stewards of this treasured species."

A photo shared by President Donald Trump from his meeting with Chinese Leader Xi Jinping has caused questions and speculation throughout the internet.
On Thursday, Trump shared the photo on his Truth Social platform . In it, the president stands next to Xi, with Trump’s arm raised in a salute. The words “Only Trump” are in the picture as the two leaders stand in the foreground at the front of the red carpet with Xi’s plane in the background. Overhead, a military plane flies past the scene.
A lone woman is also caught in the picture. Some on the internet have speculated that is was Trump’s personal aide Natalie Harp . But the woman is Chief of Protocol Monica Crowley , a former Fox News anchor who joined the Trump administration.
Others have questioned if the photo was made by AI. Trump was mocked for flinching during the flyover, and was caught by cameras clenching his teeth and ducking his head . Others pointed out other issues with the picture, such as Trump missing a glove on one hand, but it appearing in other pictures from the event. In addition, the shoes Crowley was seen wearing in the original Reuters photograph – similar to Mary Janes with a horizontal strap across the top – appear to have been changed to classic nude-colored pumps in the picture posted on Truth Social.
Notably absent from the picture shared on Truth Social was first lady Melania Trump, who was also present at the event.
A number of social media users questioned whether the photo had been manipulated, whether through AI or other means.
“Why take the glove off his left hand??” wrote one X user. In pictures taken by photojournalists, the president can be seen wearing two black gloves.
“There’s a lot of slop,” another user chimed in.
“He AI edited out his wife but left Natalie?” questioned a third user, though the woman in the photo is actually Crowley.
Crowley has served as U.S. chief of protocol since 2025, advising the president on diplomatic protocol.
She has accompanied Trump during other meetings with other world leaders, including King Charles III and Queen Camilla . She also traveled with Trump to Beijing for his state visit in May.
On Thursday, Trump and Xi struck a positive tone about their relationship and outlined areas for cooperation as the state visit got underway.
“From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people,” Trump said. He added that the two leaders would discuss artificial intelligence and other pressing issues.
Xi said he and Trump had established a “personal rapport” and called for closer diplomatic ties in order to bring about a peaceful coexistence.
“It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses,” the Chinese leader said.
An earlier version of this story and headline incorrectly identified the person in the photo as Donald Trump's personal aide Natalie Harp. The person in the frame is Chief of Protocol Monica Crowley.

Appearing before lawmakers on Thursday, President Donald Trump ’s nominee to head the Food and Drug Administration defended the safety of established immunizations, even as senators pressed her on White House attempts to alter routine childhood vaccination schedules.
Dr. Heidi Overton, a physician serving as an adviser in the White House, has helped shape several health policies for the administration. Among them was an executive order signed last month recommending that long-standing childhood vaccines be separated and spaced out over time.
Overton was present alongside Trump in the Oval Office when he made the false claim that the combined measles, mumps and rubella shot could prove "quite lethal."
Sen. Bill Cassidy , the physician from Louisiana who chairs the Senate Health Committee, urged Overton to refute that claim and publicly confirm the safety of FDA -cleared vaccines.
Overton told lawmakers that "Right now every vaccine that is on the market has been determined to be safe and effective," explicitly citing the MMR shot.
Cassidy has consistently sought pledges from health officials nominated by Trump to preserve established vaccine standards, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., despite the administration continuing to advance measures that weaken public confidence in immunization.
"Kennedy gave me guarantees, and he did not keep them," the Louisiana Republican stated. "If the president asks you to do something that goes against those guarantees you give us today, what will you do?"
Responding to the panel, Overton stated she would "follow the statutory requirements" governing agency commissioners while offering Trump her honest advice.
As questioning continued, she stopped short of directly stating that Trump was mistaken regarding MMR vaccine safety.
"This committee needs to know whether you will be radically honest, whether you will use your authority to stand up for sound science and protect children’s health," Cassidy told her.
The chairman did not say if he planned to endorse her confirmation or set a date for a vote.
Should she win confirmation, Overton will take over several contentious agency initiatives, such as an ongoing evaluation of the country's primary abortion medication and updated regulations easing sales of flavored e-cigarettes.
These topics drew significant attention from both Democratic and Republican members of the committee.
The nominee also faced scrutiny regarding her previous comments on reproductive healthcare.
The FDA originally authorized the abortion medication mifepristone in 2000 and has reaffirmed its safety profile over the years while expanding distribution options, including mail delivery.
However, Kennedy directed the agency to conduct a fresh safety evaluation last year after pressure from anti-abortion organizations and conservative legislators.
During her tenure at the conservative America First Policy Institute, Overton authored a piece labeling the decision to permit mail-order mifepristone as "dangerous to women," characterizing the policy as facilitating "chemical abortion on demand."
Under questioning from Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, Overton avoided detailing her personal opinions on mifepristone, noting that the medication "has met the safety and efficacy determinations of the FDA." She added that she preferred not to "prejudge" the review currently underway at the agency.
"The FDA has said this is safe," Murray, a Democrat, countered. "We need someone in FDA to make sure this is done by science."
Republican members on the committee, led by Cassidy, recently released a report alleging that the small group of companies distributing mifepristone might be failing to follow guidelines concerning the oversight of prescribing physicians.
"If I’m confirmed as commissioner, I would be committed to making sure every company is following the law," Overton stated in response to Indiana Republican Sen. Jim Banks.
Her stance on abortion could make securing votes from moderate Republicans on the committee more challenging, specifically Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.
Both senators have broken rank with their party to support abortion access, with Collins currently facing a competitive reelection battle where reproductive rights remain a defining topic.
During Thursday's hearing, however, Collins chose to press Overton on another matter: recent actions by the FDA approving new flavored electronic cigarettes.
In earlier presidential terms, including Trump's initial presidency, the agency restricted sweet-flavored vaping products over concerns about youth appeal.
Overton defended the decisions by explaining that FDA scientific staff endorsed the approval of several fruit-flavored devices after concluding they satisfied the regulatory test of being "appropriate for the protection of public health" by aiding adults in quitting smoking.
"They believed that standard was met because so many adult smokers are using flavors preferentially," Overton explained.
Securing the top position will require Overton to gain majority support from the 21 members of the health panel before advancing to a full Senate vote.
Directing the agency under the present administration demands navigating competing priorities, matching Trump's mandate to roll back regulatory burdens on products like e-cigarettes against Kennedy’s focus on re-examining vaccines, pharmaceuticals, and food ingredients.
Similar institutional tensions previously led to the resignation of former agency head Dr. Marty Makary in May. Makary's brief tenure was marked by internal leadership shifts, scientific disagreements, and widespread reports highlighting plummeting workplace morale and organizational turmoil. Since Trump assumed office, workforce reductions, buyouts, retirements, and resignations have trimmed the agency's total staff by roughly 20%.
Overton previously studied under Makary at Johns Hopkins University, earning a doctorate in clinical research after completing her medical degree at the University of New Mexico.
Much like her former mentor, Overton lacks prior experience leading a massive agency, a key requirement for overseeing 16,000 employees located across domestic and international offices.
Financial disclosures show Overton holds no equity in food or healthcare corporations—a notable departure from Makary and previous candidates for the position, many of whom were forced to sell off assets or sever financial links with entities overseen by the regulator.
Her filings listed between $50,000 and $100,000 in outstanding student debt.

articles.title_orig: How the Hell Did American Stealth Fighter Parts “Inexplicably” Make Their Way to China?
articles.title_zh: How the Hell Did American Stealth Fighter Parts “Inexplicably” Make Their Way to China?
articles.content_orig:
The Pentagon is investigating how a shipment of F-35 fighter jet parts on its way to the U.S. from overseas was diverted, and the military is now trying to retrieve the parts, a defense official confirmed to CBS News.
A source briefed on the incident told CBS News a shipment was diverted to Hong Kong. According to Bloomberg News , the parts are now in China's hands, although the Pentagon declined to confirm this.
A defense official said in a statement, "The F-35 Joint Program Office and Department of War are aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components." The parts were in transit to the U.S. from Australia either for replacement or repair when they were diverted.
"We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence," the defense official said.
The F-35A Lightning II is the newest version of the plane and the most advanced fighter jet in the military's arsenal. It travels up to 1,200 miles per hour and can carry a payload of 18,000 pounds.
The missing parts are said to be related to the plane's canopy and weapons bay door. If this is the case, they do not contain the kind of advanced avionics that would be advantageous for an adversary to obtain. Nonetheless, they could provide information about the F-35's stealth technology: Even the canopy contains elements of the stealth systems — it's coated with radar-absorbent material that helps the plane hide from enemy radar.
It's not clear whether the U.S. raised the missing plane parts with China during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit with President Trump on Thursday, but military issues almost certainly came up during their meeting. Xi was expected to press Mr. Trump to curb U.S. support for Taiwan. China wants the U.S. to halt all arms sales to the self-governed island and oppose Taiwanese independence.
Doing so would effectively end the longstanding policy of strategic ambiguity, that is, refusing to state whether the U.S. would intervene militarily if China were to attack Taiwan.
After their summit in May, Mr. Trump said he had made "no commitment either way" on whether to move forward with a pending arms sale to Taiwan. Democratic and Republican lawmakers have urged him to approve the arms package, but it has remained in limbo since Mr. Trump and Xi last met.
On Wednesday, Republican Sens. Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn and Lisa Murkowski wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to ask why the State Department did not obligate $300 million in foreign military financing Congress had approved for 2026 and the Defense Department did not provide Taiwan with $1 billion appropriated by Congress for security cooperation. They also wanted to know why the administration did not approve the $14 billion in military sales to Taiwan that Congress passed earlier this year.
The senators said in their letter that the appropriations "are critical to the kind of deterrence by denial that will prevent conflict," and said "it is especially confusing that the Administration would withhold approval of the very arms purchases it aggressively pushed Taiwan to make."
Ed  O'Keefe and Anna  Coren contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Bond yields surge to fresh two-decade highs but oil prices buffeted by Iran headlines
articles.title_zh: Bond yields surge to fresh two-decade highs but oil prices buffeted by Iran headlines
articles.content_orig:
Key U.S. Treasury yields surged to fresh two-decade highs Thursday, as the price of oil jumped to as high as $108 per barrel.
The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond soared as high as 5.47%, a level not seen in 22 years.
After posting its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond continued advancing on Thursday. In early trading it climbed as high as 5.18%. That remains its highest level since 2007.
Due to the influence that the 10-year yield has over consumer borrowing rates, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped to 7.37% on Thursday, its highest level since May 2024.
Meanwhile, oil prices jumped again overnight after a mediated U.S. dialogue with Iran at the United Nations General Assembly produced no tangible evidence of any progress toward ending the seven-month war.
Much of the day’s gains in oil were reversed shortly after midday Eastern time, following a Reuters report that U.S. and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased path out of the war. The path reportedly involves Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters’ multiple unnamed sources.
NBC News has not confirmed the Reuters report.
The reversal was short lived, however, and international Brent crude oil continued rising and closed higher by 3.4% at $106.60. U.S. crude oil ended the day higher by 2.6% at $94.61 per barrel.
Since the start of the year, both Brent and West Texas Intermediary crude are up more than 65%.
Those rising oil prices have continued to push commercial diesel fuel prices to all-time records. On Thursday, the national average price for diesel was $6.51, effectively unchanged from a day earlier, but up 73% since the Iran war began.
Likewise, the national average price of regular unleaded gas was 50% higher Thursday than it when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, at $4.48 per gallon.
Stocks fell in early trading, but like oil, sharply reversed course on the Reuters report. The S&P 500 erased a drop of 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite erased a 0.9% slip. Both indexes closed flat.
Around the world, the bond sell-off is roiling sovereign debt markets.
“The acceleration higher in US rates yesterday is being felt globally as to highlight for the umpteenth time that we’re all in this global bond boat together,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth.
The yield on Japan’s 10-year bond rose to its highest level since 1996 on Thursday, while Germany’s 10-year bund notched its highest yield since 2009.
“As summer officially ends, macro data are still fairly solid in the US, as indicated by a 4%-type unemployment rate and 2%-ish growth,” wrote Bank of America’s global rates analysts.
“But the risks continue to pile up for anxious markets,” they added, pointing to ongoing trade wars, the energy supply shock, upcoming midterm elections and potential risks to the AI boom.
One major driver of the surge in bond yields this week was a report from S&P Global, released Wednesday morning, that found that while U.S. business activity accelerated in September, “firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher.”
That led investors and traders to ramp up their bets on Fed rate hikes.
Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said the central bank still has more work to do to help bring down inflation.
It’s “likely that another rate hike may be appropriate by the end of the year,” Williams said during a speech in London Thursday.
Nonetheless, he said, the U.S. economy has demonstrated “remarkable resilience” in the face of “significant shocks” hitting it.
Another key official, Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed , said Thursday that she too expects “some modest further tightening may be warranted.”
In central banker parlance, tightening refers to raising rates.
The rise in bond yields has continued despite a series of measures taken — and warnings delivered — by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month.
“ I am the house now, ” Bessent said on Sept. 8, “and you can bet against me if you want.”
At the time, Bessent was defending a Treasury Department intervention to help prop up the Japanese yen. The hope was that a stronger yen would relieve pressure on the Japanese government to sell U.S. Treasury bonds.
But it hasn’t entirely worked, and as of Thursday, the Japanese yen had again weakened to levels on par with it’s exchange rate against the U.S. dollar from early September.
Bessent has also intervened in the U.S. bond markets, buying back longer-dated Treasurys in an effort to keep their yields low.
In response to the department’s initial buyback earlier this month, bond yields rose — exactly the opposite reaction from what the administration intended.
But Bessent has brushed off the stumble, insisting that the U.S. bond market is still the “best performing” in the world and crediting President Donald Trump for it.
“If some of the Bloomberg Terminal bros are unhappy with what I’m doing, well, that’s too bad,” Bessent said in an interview on Sept. 10.
The second round of Bessent’s buyback plan was conducted Thursday, when the Treasury bought back about $4 billion worth of 20- and 30-year bonds. As with the initial round, yields rose to their highest level of the session on the news —  but the jump was far less notable than it had been a month ago.
“Mechanically, today’s operation went more smoothly,” said Brian Rehling, co-head of of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo. But “long-end yields are still being set by inflation, Fed expectations,” and the volume of debt being issued.
“Today’s operation is unlikely to alter the trajectory of long-term interest rates, which we believe will continue to move higher until the market believes inflation is being brought under control,” he added.
“US Treasury Secretary ‘House’ Bessent seems to be demonstrating the house does not always win,” wrote Paul Donovan, the chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, on Thursday morning.
CORRECTION (Sept. 24, 2026, 2:19 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misstated Thursday’s national average price for diesel. It was $6.51, not $4.51.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_zh: Trump hails friendship with Xi as China's leader urges ‘healthy' competition between 2 powers
